lens/overview.title: Using AI to Connect Every Route to Our Data
lens/overview.text: Using AI to make data and insight easier to find, with one assistant across the platform. This case study is password protected; ask Tobi for access.

lens-platform/overview.title: Analytics That Hold Up at a Million Rows
lens-platform/overview.text: Redesigning tables, charts, maps and navigation for an enterprise analytics platform. This case study is password protected; ask Tobi for access.

hydra/overview.title: Hydra: When Banks Speak Five Different Languages
hydra/overview.text: A B2B API gateway that pulls fragmented banking integrations into one dashboard, cutting integration time and giving fintechs one bill instead of five. Client: Qore Technologies. Role: Sole Product Designer. Project Type: Web. Timeline: 2 Months. The challenge: Fintech developers and bank partners had to stitch together fragmented B2B APIs by hand, separate bills, separate dashboards, and configuration errors that showed up only after launch. The solution: We built Hydra, a single B2B API gateway dashboard that shows payload structure clearly, streamlines credential setup, and puts every provider's billing in one place.

hydra/control-center.title: The Control Center for Connected Finance
hydra/control-center.text: The project: Over a fast two-month timeline, I owned the end-to-end design for Hydra, a platform Qore Technologies built to pull together scattered financial APIs for banks and fintechs into one place. The dilemma: The tool had to work for two very different people at once, engineers reading raw data logs, and bank office staff checking bills and transaction histories. Neither could feel like an afterthought. Engineers. Reading raw data logs and configuring keys.. Audience 1. Bank office staff. Checking bills and transaction histories.. Audience 2 What we did: I replaced confusing charts with a clean, filter-driven view and moved technical documentation directly into the workspace. Engineers and business managers could finally use the same tool without stepping on each other.

hydra/sorting-the-mess.title: Sorting the Mess: Organizing Scattered Bank Tools
hydra/sorting-the-mess.text: The chaos before Hydra: Financial institutions bought payment processing, balance checks, and transaction tracking from separate vendors, each with its own code style, its own bill, its own messy spreadsheet export. For the people using it daily, that was three jobs pretending to be one. Payment processing. Own vendor, own code style, own bill.. Vendor A. Balance checks. Own vendor, own code style, own bill.. Vendor B. Transaction tracking. Own vendor, own spreadsheet export.. Vendor C. Hydra pulled all of them into one place. Mapping it out: I ran a card-sorting exercise with real users to see how they actually grouped information, which shaped a navigation system built on how people think, not how the APIs happened to be structured. The team. 1 designer (me). 1 project manager. 1 product manager. 3 engineers. 2-month timeline Working the constraints: I was the only designer on a team with a project manager, a product manager, and three engineers, which meant daily trade-offs. I led a workshop to build a low-fidelity wireframe for the Hydra dashboard, quick enough to iterate on and honest enough to get real feedback before we committed to anything.

hydra/dashboards-code-lookups.title: Redesigning Dashboards and Code Lookups
hydra/dashboards-code-lookups.text: Where developers kept tripping: In testing, developers could manage security keys but couldn't see the actual structure of the data those keys unlocked. They kept leaving the app to check external docs, which broke their focus every time. The pivot: Our first analytics screens used multi-coloured circle charts. Users found them confusing and tiring for daily work. We stripped them out for plain line graphs and simple dropdown filters, so isolating a date range or a transaction problem took seconds, not guesswork. Before. After. Multi-coloured circle charts. Plain line graphs. Hard to read daily. Simple dropdown filters for date range and issues. Docs in another tab. Code structure in a slide-out drawer on the same screen The code panel: I built a slide-out drawer directly into the key configuration screen. Click a security key, and the exact code structure slides open on the same screen, no tab-switching required. A trade-off worth naming: Engineering flagged that a live payload preview would mean an expensive API call every time the drawer opened, slowing the whole dashboard down. I compromised with local JSON schema caching, showing structural mock payloads instantly client-side and saving live calls for final validation only. Live payload preview. What we shipped. Expensive API call every time the drawer opened. Local JSON schema caching. Slower dashboard. Structural mock payloads, shown instantly Stress-testing the interface: Financial dashboards live or die on how they handle volume. I built interactive Figma prototypes simulating extreme cases, tables with thousands of rows, to polish spacing and row layout, and to catch where long numbers would cut off, before a single line of code was written. Talking to the people who'd use it: Over a focused week, I ran usability tests over Figma and Microsoft Teams with enterprise admins and developers. Admins consistently said the same thing, watched: the unified billing view was clear, but seeing projected costs based on current usage would make monthly planning much easier. I turned that feedback directly into the layout: help documentation embedded in the sidebars, standardised status badges, and a predictive monthly cost projection view.

hydra/results.title: From Fragmented APIs to ₦60M+ in Processed Transactions
hydra/results.text: Accessibility: Every financial data table, status badge, and billing display was checked against WCAG 2.1 AA, so dense content, transaction histories, API configurations, billing records, stayed legible and navigable for users relying on assistive technology. 46%. faster developer integration. 38%. fewer billing entry errors. 45+. partner fintechs and banks onboarded. ₦60M+. processed securely since launch

qore/overview.title: Qore: 500 Banks, One Afternoon Each
qore/overview.text: A no-code setup wizard that lets African microfinance banks configure and launch a fully branded banking app, cutting deployment from months to a single afternoon across 500+ institutions. Client: Qore Technologies. Role: Lead Product Designer. Project Type: Web & Mobile. Timeline: 5 Months. The challenge: Microfinance banks across Africa faced months of manual development just to launch a digital app, and what came out the other end was often visually broken, inaccessible, and shed customers at sign-up. The solution: We built a no-code setup wizard that lets a bank operator configure their brand inside a locked-down token system, paired with a 2-minute customer onboarding flow.

qore/zero-to-deploy.title: Banking Apps for Africa: The Zero-to-Deploy Playbook
qore/zero-to-deploy.text: The big picture: I owned the complete product design for a multi-tenant platform letting banks across Africa, large and small, launch a fully branded web and mobile banking app without months of custom code. The balancing act: Bank stakeholders wanted total styling freedom to make their app look distinct. We needed strict layout limits to keep every one of those apps accessible, secure, and bug-free for everyday consumers. Those two goals fight each other by default. My approach: I built a linear, step-by-step setup wizard. A non-technical bank operator could pick a theme, map their corporate colours, and generate a downloadable, testable preview of their app without touching a developer. Pick a theme. Map brand colours. Preview the app. Downloadable and testable.. Deploy. No developer needed.

qore/white-label-engine.title: Untangling Legacy Code into a Core White-Label Engine
qore/white-label-engine.text: What we inherited: Every new bank used to trigger a manual build cycle, months of engineering delay for each one. The resulting apps were slow and cluttered, with onboarding drop-off at 45% and little user trust to show for the wait. Two very different users: I structured discovery around two groups with genuinely different mental models. Bank administrators went through expert interviews and stakeholder mapping, which surfaced the friction in their existing branding workflow. Consumers went through usability tests against competing white-label apps to find precise drop-off moments. Card sorting with both groups validated our navigation and revealed the real split: operators wanted control, consumers wanted speed and reassurance. Splitting the system in two: I broke the platform into two distinct spaces: Management Layer. Dashboard for bank admins: branding, permissions, configuration.. For admins. Customer Application Core. Standardised flow for transfers, bill payments and expense tracking.. For customers

qore/management-layer.title: The Management Layer: Configuration and Customization Dashboard
qore/management-layer.text: Admin control center: The Management Layer gives bank administrators one clear dashboard for branding setup, user permissions, styling variables, and live configuration. No-code branding: Operators test colour choices, manage logo placement, adjust corner radius, and pick typography live, before anything deploys.

qore/customer-app-core.title: The Customer Application Core: Optimizing White-Label Onboarding
qore/customer-app-core.text: Built for everyday banking: The Customer Application Core is a standardised, fast flow for transfers, bill payments, and expense tracking. Rebuilding onboarding: Our work on the consumer app centred on cutting sign-up steps and the friction that came with them. Under two minutes: Account opening now takes under two minutes. We kept only the fields that actually matter, so customers start transacting sooner, and a fast, easy start tells them they picked the right bank.

qore/token-blueprint.title: Aligning the Team & The Token Blueprint
qore/token-blueprint.text: A strict rule, agreed with engineering: Structural layouts stayed locked to prevent bugs. Visual properties were treated as dynamic variables. Getting product and engineering to agree on that split up front saved months of arguments later. Locked. Flexible. Structural layout. Colours (on safe surfaces only). Spacing and hierarchy. Logo placement. Base palette: grey, white, black. Corner radius and typography Dynamic tokens: We used Figma Variables, exported through Style Dictionary into a shared config file engineers could plug straight into their codebase. Built to scale: With that token ecosystem in place, a change to a colour value, spacing parameter, or component style compiled automatically across every micro-site and white-labeled module, no manual developer touch needed. Figma Variables. Style Dictionary. Shared config file. Every bank's app. Updates compile automatically.

qore/color-problem.title: The Color Problem: Protecting Readability in a White-Labeled World
qore/color-problem.text: The dilemma: Give business clients full control over styling, and they'll often pick vibrant, clashing colour combinations. In early testing, those custom palettes broke WCAG 2.1 AA outright, making financial figures unreadable for end-users. What went wrong first: Our first pass let admins apply any colour to any button or background text. It broke layouts and created real visual bugs. Unstructured freedom, it turned out, compromised the safety of the product itself. The fix: I pivoted to a monochrome-base scaling pattern. The foundational layout stayed anchored to grey, white, and black. A bank's brand colours were injected only into specific, safe surfaces, action buttons, active tabs, success screens. Full accessibility, any corporate identity.

qore/results.title: Shifting from Months of Code to Instant Scaling
qore/results.text: Replacing manual engineering with an automated config tool delivered results fast: 4 mo → 1 afternoon. to launch a bank's app. 45% → <8%. onboarding failure. 500+. microfinance banks powered. <2 min. to open an account

mamvest/overview.title: MAMVest: From a Three-Day Wire Transfer to Under Four Minutes
mamvest/overview.text: A digital wealth platform that opens Mutual Funds, Bonds, and Treasury Bills to retail investors, replacing a paper-bound process that used to take days. Client: Mango Asset Management. Role: Lead Product Designer. Project Type: Web & Mobile. Timeline: 4 Months. The challenge: Mango Asset Management ran on paperwork, physical prospectuses, manual KYC checks, wire verification by hand, a workflow that took 3 to 5 business days for a single transaction. The solution: We built MAMVest, an SEC-approved digital wealth platform that opens Mutual Funds, Bonds, Treasury Bills, and Commercial Papers to retail investors from as little as ₦1,000, and cut transaction time to under 4 minutes.

mamvest/legacy-institution.title: Re-Engineering a Legacy Institution: Designing the First Digital Wealth Platform
mamvest/legacy-institution.text: The big picture: For decades, Mango Asset Management managed premium portfolios for corporate clients and high-net-worth individuals through paperwork, relationship managers, and offline operations. To reach retail investors, the firm committed to a 4-month push to build MAMVest, their first customer-facing digital product. Approved by Nigeria's SEC, the platform opens up Mutual Funds, Bonds, Treasury Bills, Commercial Papers, and liquidity tools to retail investors, with an entry point as low as ₦1,000. What retail investors can now access, from ₦1,000. Mutual Funds. Bonds. Treasury Bills. Commercial Papers. Liquidity tools The tension: We had to take compliance-heavy, paper-bound investment processes and turn them into something light enough for a mobile-first generation, without losing the decades of institutional trust the brand had built. My role: As Lead Product Designer, I owned design strategy, visual governance, and cross-platform architecture across three products, the customer mobile app (React Native), the web portal, and the internal Admin Control Desk. Leading a team of three designers, my job went beyond screens: managing stakeholders across departments, mapping the end-to-end service blueprint, running research and testing, and building a design-to-code pipeline that wouldn't rack up technical debt as we scaled. 3 products: app, web, Admin Control Desk. Team of 3 designers. 4-month timeline. 5-day alignment sprint

mamvest/service-blueprint.title: From Paper to Pixels: Service Blueprinting & Cross-Functional Alignment
mamvest/service-blueprint.text: What was actually broken: When someone wanted to put money into a Commercial Paper or a Bond, the process took 3 to 5 business days: a physical prospectus, KYC signed by post or courier, bank wire verification, and an account officer logging it all by hand into a spreadsheet. Physical prospectus. KYC by post or courier. Bank wire verification. Manual logging by an account officer. Total: 3 to 5 business days to invest. Mapping it end to end: To break down the silos causing that delay, I built a Service Blueprint that lined up what the customer saw (frontstage) against what Mango's teams actually did behind it (backstage), compliance checks, clearinghouse timing, banking settlement rails. Once that dependency chain was visible, it was obvious where automation belonged, and where it would just break something. Getting the whole company aligned: I ran a 5-day alignment sprint with the firm's leadership, the Product Management Director, Head of Engineering, Compliance Directors, and senior portfolio managers who'd run the paper-based version for years. Using a Lean Canvas, I anchored the direction to actual business metrics rather than opinions about what looked good. We landed on one rule that held the whole project together: legal disclosure stayed locked for compliance, but the data-entry path around it got optimised hard.

mamvest/design-system.title: The 3-Tier Design System & Token Architecture
mamvest/design-system.text: One source of truth, three tech stacks: Building for Flutter (iOS and Android) and Tailwind (web) at the same time, I set up a 3-tier design system so engineering handoff didn't lag and the UI didn't drift apart across platforms. We kept the token repository in a single JSON file, distributed via Style Dictionary straight into production. Single JSON token file. Style Dictionary. Flutter (iOS + Android). Tailwind (web) Making the catalogue make sense: To stop retail investors drowning in institutional jargon, my team restructured Mango's product offering into a clean, unified taxonomy:

mamvest/stress-testing.title: High-Density Stress Testing & Real-World Layout Scaling
mamvest/stress-testing.text: Testing for the worst day, not the best one: Over the four months, I put our Figma prototypes through deliberate stress testing, astronomical balances (₦180,500,750.22), deep multi-asset histories, fractional interest values, dropped network calls. That work made sure layout containers expanded properly, typography scaled cleanly, and no number ever clipped, even on a budget phone with a low-resolution screen.

mamvest/results.title: Business Performance & Systemic Transformation Impact
mamvest/results.text: Replacing paper-bound workflows with a proper digital architecture changed Mango's position in the market, in four months: 3–5 days → 3m 42s. to discover, clear compliance and invest. 54% → 11%. onboarding abandonment. 40%. faster secondary feature builds. ₦1,000. minimum entry point The Admin Control Desk: Built for Mango's relationship managers and compliance officers, this gives real-time visibility into KYC status, subscription activity, and audit trails. Centralising that work replaced a manual spreadsheet process that used to take 3 to 5 business days to reconcile, freeing account officers to service more clients at once.

moore/overview.title: Moore: Banking That Doesn't Feel Like Banking
moore/overview.text: A digital banking app that cut onboarding drop-off from 48% to 14% and turned a heavy banking backend into something that feels warm and fast, even on a slow connection. Client: Moore. Role: Founding Designer. Project Type: Web & Mobile. Timeline: 5 Months. The challenge: Moore's onboarding had eight stages, its web and mobile screens didn't look like the same product, and every time the network dropped mid-transaction, users assumed the app had crashed and them lost their money. The solution: We cut onboarding to three validated steps, aligned the web and mobile layouts to one set of rules, and built a payment progress engine people could actually trust. That combination took Moore to 8,000+ organic downloads and a Friends & Family seed round.

moore/visual-flow.title: Establishing the End-to-End Visual & Interaction Flow
moore/visual-flow.text: The role: As founding product designer, I owned the end-to-end experience and visual direction for Moore. The idea was simple to say and hard to build: fold sending money, savings, and everyday finance into one app that felt like it belonged in a new market, not a scaled-down version of a Western bank app. The tension: Underneath a warm, welcoming surface sat genuinely heavy banking infrastructure. The job was to hide that weight without hiding the trust that comes with knowing your money is safe, on phones that weren't fast and networks that weren't stable. Working with the founders: I sat with the founding team to map the primary flows across web and mobile, aligning the two so a transaction felt like the same action wherever you tapped it.

moore/onboarding.title: Optimizing Onboarding: Redesigning Sign-Up Friction
moore/onboarding.text: What I inherited: When I joined, the app felt like three products stitched together. New users were quitting mid sign-up, drop-off sat at 48%, and there was no shared foundation to launch on different phones or in new languages without rebuilding from scratch. Cutting eight stages to five: I compressed the sign-up flow from eight stages to five, with real-time validation against standard input guidelines so an error got caught before submission, not after. Before. After. 8 sign-up stages. 5 sign-up stages. Errors caught after submission. Real-time validation as you type. 48% drop-off. 14% drop-off Designing the website alongside the app: I pushed to design the public marketing site at the same time as the mobile product. The bet was that if people understood what the app did before they downloaded it, we'd lower acquisition cost and cut cold-start friction. It worked.

moore/payment-experience.title: Removing Fear: Designing a Stress-Free Payment Experience
moore/payment-experience.text: A mistake worth naming: Our first payment screens used a standard spinning loader. Watching real people use it, the opposite of calm happened; a blank spinner made them anxious. Most assumed the app had frozen and backed out mid-transfer. The fix: We threw the spinner out and built a step-by-step progress tracker that names exactly what's happening, in real time. PIN entry sits in its own clear space, a light vibration confirms every tap, and the transfer summary shows up right before you hit send, not after. Live progress tracker. Names exactly what's happening, in real time.. PIN in its own space. Clear, uncluttered entry.. Haptic confirmation. A light vibration on every tap.. Summary before send. See the transfer before it goes.

moore/tokenized-system.title: Tokenizing the Visual System: Aligning Cross-Platform Layouts
moore/tokenized-system.text: One system, three platforms: To scale Moore across iOS, Android, and web without three separate visual languages, I turned the early layouts into a proper component library, one that stayed consistent and was easy to update without touching every screen by hand. Tokens linked to code. Figma variables mapped to developer components; layout identical across iOS, Android and web.. Worst-case testing. Bad networks and balances like ₦2,905,215.23, so nothing clips.. Accessibility built in. WCAG 2.1 AA contrast, minimum font sizes, older Android phones.. Engineers, not around them. One shared library and token set, so screens shipped without drift. Read about our post-design-system Figma variables & AI accessibility presentation at UX Scotland

moore/results.title: Proven Growth & Performance Results
moore/results.text: 48% → 14%. onboarding abandonment. 0.2%. accidental double-tap errors. ½. engineering handoff time. 8,000+. organic downloads, no paid marketing Design gates: As the team grew, I introduced Design Gates, short review checkpoints so nothing shipped without a check for errors, edge cases, and visual polish. It also gave junior designers a clear standard to work against without needing me in every review. Growth without a marketing budget: Because the product was usable and accessible from day one, Moore reached over 8,000 downloads organically, with no paid marketing behind it. What it meant for funding: Organic growth, a measurably usable product, and a real design system together helped Moore close a Friends & Family seed round. For the founding team, design wasn't decoration, it was proof to early investors that the product actually worked.

undp/overview.title: UNDP: The Panic Button That Had to Work in Four Seconds
undp/overview.text: A voice-first early-warning app for conflict zones in Northern Nigeria, letting people send a location-tagged alert with no login and no signal, in seconds. Client: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). Role: Lead UX / UI Designer. Project Type: Web & Mobile. Timeline: 3 Months. The challenge: People in conflict-prone parts of Northern Nigeria had no fast, safe way to report an emergency, and 42% had simply stopped trying. The solution: We built CEWERS, a voice-first early-warning app that sends a location-tagged alert without a login, a form, or a stable signal.

undp/digital-lifelines.title: Digital Lifelines: Rethinking Crisis Response for the United Nations
undp/digital-lifelines.text: The project: Over a fast three months for UNDP, I led the design of the Conflict Early Warning Response System, CEWERS, a web and mobile tool built to broadcast real-time safety threats across Taraba, Benue, and Nasarawa states in Northern Nigeria. The problem underneath the problem: Security teams needed detailed, accurate information to deploy help. The people reporting were under extreme stress, in physical danger, on phones with barely any signal. Those two needs pull against each other. So I stripped out the things that normally slow an app down, account registration, long forms, and built a voice-first system that gets an alert to responders without asking someone in danger to type.

undp/trust-disconnected.title: Designing for Trust Across Disconnected Areas
undp/trust-disconnected.text: The reality on the ground: 42% of local citizens had never reported an active emergency, not because nothing happened, but because the system didn't work, retaliation was a real fear, and responses were slow. Seasonal farm and land conflicts kept these communities exposed. To turn that into a working safety net, I focused on three things: Familiar landmarks. Local photos and state colours: Taraba red, Benue black, Nasarawa blue.. 1. Fewer roles, faster action. Five user types, designed around one link: Citizen → Monitor.. 2. Built for bad signal. No login, no typing: background GPS and offline storage.. 3 1. Familiar landmarks, not a generic app: Working with local governments, the app's look changes by state, custom local photos and state colours (red for Taraba, black for Benue, blue for Nasarawa) on the onboarding screens. In a high-tension environment, that recognisability builds comfort you can't fake with generic UI. 2. Fewer roles, faster action: The system supports five user types, Citizens, Monitors, Security, Observers, Admins. I focused the design on the one connection that mattered most, a Citizen sending an alert and a local Monitor validating it, and cut the middle-management steps that didn't need to be there. Five user types. Citizen ★. Monitor ★. Security. Observer. Admin. ★ The connection the design prioritised: a Citizen sends an alert, a local Monitor validates it. 3. Designing around bad signal, not against it: I made a deal with engineering: drop mandatory sign-up and typing entirely. Instead, the app leans on background GPS and offline storage. A citizen can send a location-verified alert with no login at all, the app holds the data and fires it off the second a signal reappears.

undp/panic-button.title: Designing a Stress-Free Panic Button
undp/panic-button.text: The flawed first try: The real turning point came from stress-testing an early idea. We'd built a swipeable card layout for choosing the type of emergency, land dispute, robbery, clash. The pivot: Under simulated pressure, it fell apart. People in danger get tunnel vision. Swiping through hidden options confused them, slowed them down, and made the panic worse, exactly what the app was meant to prevent. I dropped the swipe entirely and built a single-screen grid showing every alert type at once, in plain black icons. Nothing hidden, nothing to scroll for. First try: swipe cards. Final: one-screen grid. Alert types hidden behind swipes. Every alert type visible at once. Tunnel vision made it slower. Plain black icons, nothing to scroll. Typing needed for details. One-tap voice recorder: tap, speak, send Voice over text: Field data confirmed what we suspected, typing was impossible for someone running from danger, or for anyone who struggled with reading. So I put a large, one-tap voice recorder directly on the alert screen. Tap, speak, send. To keep the engine from crashing on cheap local hardware, I used Zeplin to bridge design and code, mapping global style tokens onto a lightweight Tailwind setup the front-end engineers already used. That kept the grid solid across a wide range of budget Android phones. A trade-off worth fighting for: Stakeholders originally wanted voice notes translated to text on-device before sending. On low-tier phones that processing took up to 12 seconds, a dangerous gap mid-crisis. I argued to drop on-device translation entirely and stream raw audio instead, which brought transmission down to under 2 seconds. On-device translation. What we shipped. Up to 12 seconds on low-tier phones. Raw audio sent immediately. Dangerous gap mid-crisis. Translation handled after sending Testing beyond the office: Validating an app meant to save lives can't stop at a usability lab. Alongside UNDP and local leaders, we took an Android test build into rural impact zones and ran live trials with 12 to 15 community leaders, farmers, and security workers. What the field tests told us: Three things shaped the final design.

undp/panic-button~2.title: Designing a Stress-Free Panic Button
undp/panic-button~2.text: Our alert labels were too vague under pressure, so we replaced them with bold, high-contrast warning banners that guide people step by step. Swiping between hidden categories caused real confusion during stress drills, confirming the grid pivot. And the one-tap voice recorder solved the biggest failure mode outright: people who couldn't type under duress could now file a complete, location-tagged report in under four seconds.

undp/built-to-last.title: Built to Last and Expand
undp/built-to-last.text: To make this a permanent tool rather than a one-off project, I built the components to be fully reusable. If UNDP expands this to new regions, teams onboard by swapping colours and local photos, no rewriting the underlying software. We also produced print guides written in plain, literacy-conscious language, so local governments could run community training without needing us in the room. Across every screen, WCAG-compliant contrast, large tap targets, and a voice-first primary flow kept the app usable regardless of literacy level, cognitive load, or physical environment. Proven, not theoretical: Built around how people actually behave under pressure, CEWERS was officially approved by UNDP and adopted by local Nigerian state governments, turning a tense security issue into a practical, working tool. 100%. of field-trial participants sent an alert. 95s → 4s. emergency report time. 42%. of citizens who'd never reported, now reachable without login. 12–15. community leaders, farmers and security staff in live trials

bespoka/overview.title: Bespoka: Building an Operating System for an Industry Nobody Digitised
bespoka/overview.text: A marketplace and full operating system for bespoke tailors, designed and built solo end to end, from client booking to order tracking to split-deposit invoicing. Client: Personal / Founder Project. Role: Founder, Product Designer & Builder. Project Type: Web & Mobile, Full-Stack. Timeline: Ongoing. The challenge: Bespoke tailors run real, sophisticated businesses, measurements, staged production, deposits, repeat clients, entirely on WhatsApp, memory, and paper. There's no software built around how a tailor actually works, and no way for a buyer to trust a tailor with their money and their measurements up front. The solution: I designed and built Bespoka end to end, product, interface, and the underlying backend, a two-sided platform: a public marketplace where buyers discover and book verified tailors, and a full operating system for the tailor's side of the business, from a measurement vault to a 6-stage order tracker to split-deposit invoicing.

bespoka/no-software-category.title: Designing for a Trade With No Software Category
bespoka/no-software-category.text: The gap: Every fintech I'd worked on before this had a category to sit inside, banking, wealth management, payments infrastructure. Tailoring didn't. Master tailors run genuinely complex operations, cutting schedules, fitting appointments, fabric costs, staggered deposits, and almost none of it lives anywhere but a notebook or a WhatsApp thread. Why that's a design problem, not just a market gap: When there's no existing software category to reference, there's no established interaction pattern to borrow either. I couldn't design "a CRM for tailors" by looking at how CRMs work, because a tailor's real unit of work isn't a contact record, it's a garment moving through physical stages that a spreadsheet has no language for.

bespoka/two-sided-problem.title: The Two-Sided Problem: Trust on One Side, Depth on the Other
bespoka/two-sided-problem.text: Two very different jobs under one roof: A buyer needs to trust a stranger with their body measurements and a deposit before they've seen a single stitch. A tailor needs a tool sophisticated enough to actually replace the notebook, not a simplified toy version of their real workflow. Building both into one coherent product meant neither side could compromise the other. Buyer: needs trust. Hand a stranger your measurements and a deposit before seeing a stitch.. Side 1. Tailor: needs depth. A tool real enough to replace the notebook, not a toy version.. Side 2 One design system, two audiences: I built a single navy-and-white, border-led design system, shared design tokens synced by hand between the web and mobile codebases, so the marketplace felt calm and trustworthy for a first-time buyer while the same visual language held up under the density of a real business dashboard: revenue, active orders, staff permissions, invoices.

bespoka/order-pipeline.title: The Order Pipeline as the Spine of the Product
bespoka/order-pipeline.text: Turning "trust me" into "watch it happen": The single feature I'd point to as the core of the product is the 6-stage order tracker, cutting, first fitting, sewing, quality check, and delivery. Every garment moves through it, and every stage change fires an automatic update to the client by SMS or email. Cutting. First fitting. Sewing. Quality check. Delivery. Every stage change sends the client an automatic SMS or email update. Why a tracker, not a status field: A dropdown that says "in progress" tells a client nothing. A tracker that says "fabric cut, fitting scheduled for Thursday" replaces the anxious WhatsApp check-in that every tailor I spoke to described as their biggest daily interruption. It's the same instinct behind CEWERS's field alerts or Hydra's billing view: don't make someone ask a question the system already knows the answer to. Money follows the same logic: Invoicing supports split deposits (a percentage upfront, the balance on completion) with itemised fabric, labour, and service charges, and payment links sent straight to WhatsApp, SMS, or email, because that's where tailors' clients already are, not where I'd prefer them to be.

bespoka/building-solo.title: Building It Solo, End to End
bespoka/building-solo.text: The actual craft story here: Bespoka is the first project where I've owned the whole stack myself, product decisions, interface design, and the Node/Express/Prisma backend underneath it. That's a different discipline from designing screens for someone else's engineering team to build. Every trade-off I'd normally negotiate with an engineer, I had to make and live with directly. Where that discipline shows up: subscription tiers (Free, Growth, Fashion House) are enforced server-side, not just hidden in the UI, and every tier-gated feature has to agree on both layers before I consider it done. A five-state rule runs across the whole interface, populated, empty, loading, error, and disabled, so nothing ships half-finished just because the happy path looks good in a demo. Five states on every screen. Populated. Empty. Loading. Error. Disabled

bespoka/where-it-stands.title: Where It Stands
bespoka/where-it-stands.text: Honest about the stage: Bespoka is pre-launch. There's no traction number to put here yet, and I'd rather say that plainly than dress up a seeded demo as proof. What exists instead is a complete, working product: marketplace, booking, measurements, order pipeline, invoicing, staff management, and a super-admin layer behind it, built by one person. Pricing built for how the industry actually grows: Free for a solo tailor with up to 5 clients, ₦5,000/month once a workshop needs unlimited clients and a small team, ₦15,000/month for a multi-tailor fashion house with staff permissions and marketing tools. The tiers map to how a workshop actually scales, not to arbitrary feature buckets. Free. Solo tailor, up to 5 clients.. Free. Growth. Unlimited clients and a small team.. ₦5,000/mo. Fashion House. Multi-tailor house with staff permissions and marketing tools.. ₦15,000/mo What's next: getting it in front of real tailors and buyers, and finding out which of these decisions survive contact with people who aren't me.

about/bio.title: About Me
about/bio.text: A decade into product design, the thread running through my work isn't one industry or one kind of interface. It's a habit of taking something genuinely complicated and making it usable without flattening the complexity that actually matters. "I'd rather ship something slightly rough and fix it in the open than wait for a version that never ships at all."

about/impact.title: Impact
about/impact.text: Scale: 500+ banks on one platform. Speed: 4 mo → 1 day to launch a bank's app. Growth: 11th → 3rd in its market, in three months. Conversion: 48% → 14% onboarding drop-off. Life: 95s → 4s emergency report time, UNDP. Adoption: 8,000+ organic downloads, no paid marketing.

about/principles.title: Design philosophy
about/principles.text: Kaizen: Continuous, deliberate improvement. Ship something slightly rough, watch real people use it, and fix it in the open. A version that ships and learns beats a perfect one that never does. Advocacy: The user is rarely in the meeting where decisions get made. My job is to speak for them, especially the ones easiest to forget, and to make accessibility a starting point rather than an afterthought. Durability: A design system isn't done when it works for the team that built it. It's done when other teams can pick it up, trust it, and keep building without needing me in the room. Mentorship: Good design leadership shows up in the people around you. The designers you coach and the habits you leave behind are part of the work, not a side effect of it.
